title: Disable or Modify System Firewall: Windows Host Firewall
shortTitle: Disable or Modify System Firewall: Windows Host Firewall
summary: On Windows the firewall is a host service with three profiles, named domain, private, and public, and its state and rules can be changed from several places. An attacker holding local administrator rights can turn a profile off, or add a rule that opens a port for remote access or command and control, using built-in tools such as netsh advfirewall or the PowerShell firewall cmdlets, by editing the relevant registry keys directly, or through the Windows Security interface. The artefacts are process creation records that carry those commands, registry writes under the firewall policy keys, and firewall configuration change events. Administrators and software installers touch the same controls, so the useful signals are the parent process, the scope of the new rule, and a rule that allows any address or appears outside a deployment window.

beginner.definition: The main firewall technique covers every kind of system firewall. This version is about the firewall built into Windows itself. Windows keeps three rule sets, called profiles, for domain, private, and public networks. An attacker with administrator rights can turn a profile off or add a rule.
beginner.whyItMatters: The Windows firewall blocks many incoming connections by default. If it is turned off, remote services on that machine become reachable. Attackers often open one port for their own remote control tool. This can happen quietly, because the machine keeps working as normal. A missing firewall also removes a layer that would slow an attacker down.
howItWorks: The attacker first gains administrator rights on the Windows machine, usually through a stolen account.
They check which firewall profiles are active and what rules already exist.
They disable a profile, or add a rule that opens one port to all addresses.
They can do this with a command line tool, with PowerShell, or by editing registry keys.
Windows then records events and changes in the firewall policy area of the registry.
Software installers also add rules, so you must check who created each one.
beginner.example: Picture a shared flat where every bedroom door has its own lock. The landlord keeps a list of which doors may stay open for the cleaners. A thief who lives there cannot pick the locks. Instead they change the list on the fridge. They write that the cleaners may enter any room at any time. The locks still work, and nobody hears a noise. Windows firewall rules are that list, and each edit leaves a note in the system log.
takeaways: A disabled Windows firewall profile is a clear warning sign on any host.
Check which process created a new firewall rule, and not only the rule itself.
A rule that allows all addresses is rarely needed and deserves a review.

objectives: Name the three Windows firewall profiles and explain what each one protects.
List the ways firewall settings can be changed on Windows and the traces each one leaves.
Explain how process creation records and registry events reveal firewall tampering.
Distinguish an installer's firewall rule from one added by an intruder.
Describe a review process for new or changed firewall rules on servers.
